text.paragraph: Establishing primary care for heavy daily drinking: a nonjudgmental, trauma-informed assessment, withdrawal risk and outpatient withdrawal management, thiamine, liver tests, nutrition, mood and safety, and housing, food and income [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: She wants to stop drinking before it kills her, and does not want a lecture. [S]
She is afraid of the shakes if she stops, and has nowhere steady to stay. [S]
She is worried about her liver and her weight. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Calamity Jane was born Martha Canary about 1856, perhaps on May 1, near Princeton in Mercer County, Missouri, the eldest of six children of Robert and Charlotte Canary; the 1860 census lists her as born in 1856. Many popular accounts give 1852. [D]

Her family moved to the Montana gold camps about 1864; in December 1864 a Virginia City newspaper reported the Canary girls destitute. Her mother died at Blackfoot City, Montana Territory, in 1866 and her father in Utah in 1867, leaving her an orphan of about eleven with younger brothers and sisters. [D]

After her parents' deaths she made her way alone through the railroad construction camps and military posts of Wyoming, working as a dance-hall girl, waitress and laundress, and later at work usually done by men, such as driving ox teams as a bullwhacker and hauling wood. She often wore men's clothing, including buckskins. [D]

In 1875 she joined the Newton-Jenney expedition to the Black Hills without authorization, and by 1876 she was known as Calamity Jane; how she came by the name is uncertain, and the story that an army captain named her after she saved his life is unconfirmed. [D]
In June 1876 she traveled to Deadwood in a wagon train that included James Butler (Wild Bill) Hickok, who was murdered in Deadwood on August 2, 1876. [D]
Stories of a romance or marriage between her and Hickok are legend; her biographers find that they were acquaintances for a few weeks and that no evidence supports a love affair. [R]
During a smallpox epidemic in the Black Hills in 1878 she nursed sick people, and several contemporaries and memoirists remembered her as a nurse to the sick and a helper of people in need. [D]

Her 1896 autobiographical pamphlet, Life and Adventures of Calamity Jane, By Herself, written with a ghostwriter, describes exploits as an army scout and rider that historians regard as largely imaginary. [D]

Newspapers and contemporaries repeatedly reported her heavy drinking from the 1870s on; she was arrested for intoxication and disorderly conduct, and her principal biographer writes that every effort to end her drinking failed. Her drinking, wandering and lack of money left her poor even in settled periods. [D]
Historians describe her as an alcoholic; a diagnosis in present-day terms cannot be made from the historical record. [R]
She gave birth to a son in 1882 who died soon after birth, and to a daughter in 1887. [D]
In the mid-1880s, newspapers in Rawlins, Wyoming, reported that a man she lived with, and later married, beat her and stole from her. [D]

In the 1880s and 1890s she moved from town to town in Montana, Wyoming and the Dakotas, working in hotels and saloons and hauling wood, selling copies of her pamphlet and photographs, living at times on the help of acquaintances, and for a time staying in a pest house set aside for people with communicable diseases. [D]
In 1896 she toured the northern United States with the Kohl and Middleton dime museum show. [D]

In February 1901 she fell ill on a train journey from Livingston, Montana, and, having no money, was taken to the Gallatin County poor farm at Bozeman; she was discharged within days, and afterwards she angrily denied newspaper reports that she had been a county charge. [D]

list.item: Does odd jobs, mostly cleaning, hauling and ranch work, and has always done work that most women around her did not; moves between small towns in the region for work; no steady income [S]
Staying in a spare room at a friend's house for the past month; has stayed in shelters in past winters; no health coverage; often without food at the end of the month [S]

Lost both parents before she was twelve and looked after younger siblings; a baby son died soon after birth years ago; has a grown daughter she has not seen for some time; a past partner was violent; no current partner, and she feels safe where she is staying [S]

Alcohol: about a pint of whiskey a day for years, more on binges, often starting in the morning to stop the shakes; drinks mostly alone or in bars; has stopped on her own for a few days several times and had shakes and sweats, never seizures or hallucinations [S]
Tobacco: chews tobacco daily; does not smoke; no other drugs; no opioids [S]
Wears work clothes; owns a hunting rifle [S]
Strengths: a lifetime of looking after people who are sick or down on their luck, humor and a gift for storytelling, physical toughness, friends in several towns, and her own decision to come in [S]

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert and oriented; guarded at first, then frank and funny; mild tremor and sweating; no hallucinations or confusion; mood low and tired; PHQ-9 14 with item 9 scored 0, GAD-7 11; no thoughts of suicide or self-harm. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Independent in all activities; tremor in the mornings until she drinks; works when work is offered. [S]

Vital signs recorded on 2026-03-02; see the Vital Signs section. Mental status: Alert and oriented; guarded at first, then frank and funny; mild tremor and sweating; no hallucinations or confusion; mood low and tired; PHQ-9 14 with item 9 scored 0, GAD-7 11; no thoughts of suicide or self-harm. The physical examination is limited to the findings relevant to this synthetic episode. [S]

Structured safety assessment: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent, access to means reviewed: yes. Outpatient care with daily nurse checks during withdrawal and close follow-up. Risk factors reviewed without detail: severe alcohol use disorder, depressive symptoms, early losses, past violence by a partner, housing instability and living alone at times. Firearm safety was discussed: she agreed to leave her rifle, unloaded, with her friend, who keeps it locked, during the first months of recovery. A written safety plan was made with her, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was written on the card she carries, since she has no phone. Safety is reviewed at every visit. [S]

A nonjudgmental, trauma-informed assessment: AUDIT, DSM-5-TR criteria and PEth explained as part of care, person-first language, a female clinician and a chaperone offered, consent asked before each part of the examination, and her own goals and choices first. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder (2018); The Healthcare Professional's Core Resource on Alcohol (2026); Unhealthy Alcohol Use in Adolescents and Adults: Screening and Behavioral Counseling Interventions (2018) [S]

Addiction medicine consultation to confirm the diagnosis, review withdrawal and choose a medicine for alcohol use disorder. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder (2018); The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020) [S]

Outpatient withdrawal management at low risk (PAWSS 3, CIWA-Ar 9): a five-day gabapentin schedule, daily nurse checks with the CIWA-Ar in person or by the clinic phone, her friend as support, fluids and food; hospital care at once for a CIWA-Ar of 15 or more, a seizure, hallucinations, confusion or vomiting. Guideline: The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020) [S]

Thiamine 100 mg by injection for three days, then by mouth, with folic acid, potassium and magnesium replacement. Guideline: The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020); Diagnosis and Treatment of Alcohol-Associated Liver Diseases: 2019 Practice Guidance From the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (2019) [S]

Liver: FIB-4 of 3.93, so transient elastography; liver enzymes, albumin, INR and platelets followed; hepatitis A and B vaccination; acetaminophen no more than 2 g a day. Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Alcohol-Associated Liver Diseases: 2019 Practice Guidance From the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (2019) [S]

Mood and safety: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 again after two to four weeks without alcohol before deciding on depression treatment; a structured safety assessment, a written safety plan, the rifle stored with her friend, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety review at every visit. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder (2018); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Recovery support and harm reduction: weekly contact with the clinic's peer recovery support specialist, her choice of mutual-help meetings (Alcoholics Anonymous, SMART Recovery or Women for Sobriety), and a plan for a return to drinking: call the peer specialist or the clinic, eat, do not drink alone or drive, keep taking any medicine for alcohol use disorder, and come back without shame. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder (2018); The Healthcare Professional's Core Resource on Alcohol (2026) [S]

Housing, food, income and coverage: the clinic's community health worker helps with a Montana Medicaid application, SNAP benefits, a food bank, the local Human Resource Development Council's housing programs, Montana 211, and a free phone through the Lifeline program. Guideline: The Healthcare Professional's Core Resource on Alcohol (2026) [S]

Alcohol and women's health: why the same amount of alcohol does women more harm (higher blood alcohol, faster liver damage, a higher breast cancer risk), a pregnancy test, contraception if needed, and breast and cervical cancer screening at the preventive visit. Guideline: The Healthcare Professional's Core Resource on Alcohol (2026) [S]
Chewing tobacco: advice to stop and nicotine replacement offered whenever she is ready. Guideline: Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021) [S]
Referral to addiction medicine, Dolores Two Bulls-Harmon, MD, ordered 2026-03-02 [S]
